item.title: When the Mind Doesn’t Return From War
item.description:
Trauma

When the Mind Doesn’t Return From War

Why, for many who spent time in warzones, past trauma invades the present.

Posted August 17, 2026

Key points
  • The mind often returns to what has shaped us most—but often, that place can be the hardest to leave.
  • Individuals who spent time in warzones often find it especially difficult to leave those experiences behind.
  • Many are struggling with PTSD; for others, PTSD does not fully explain the challenges they face.
  • Healing begins when you recognise how the past continues to shape the present.

When you think back to your first heartbreak, it is striking how vividly those feelings can return. Even after years have passed, some painful events can feel as though they happened only yesterday, collapsing time and distance in an instant.

That was true for AJ (not his real name). According to The Guardian:

The faces of the two young Afghan policemen would never leave him [AJ]. They had both been shot while defending their position and bled to death in the back of a trailer as AJ and a medic tried to staunch their wounds. They could not have been more than 17 years old.

AJ is a former Royal Marine who served in Afghanistan. Just as the faces of the two young policemen never seemed to leave him, many service personnel return home carrying memories that continue to haunt them. As The Guardian observed, many of them are "damaged not by a traumatic event, but by the shock of returning from war." They came home but could not find the home they left behind,

The Psychological Cost of Returning Home From War

Many ex-servicemen and women return from war with insomnia, anxiety, intrusive memories, hallucinations, a severe sense of isolation, and guilt about what they did, didn't do, or could have done.

AJ now lives in Exeter, England, but part of him still feels as though he had never left Afghanistan. As The Guardian reported:

He was assigned a role as an instructor, but as he lectured classes on preparing orders for battle, he would suddenly find himself back on the tower in Robinson, braced for a fresh barrage of mortar rounds. He only realised he had trailed off in mid-sentence when his audience began to murmur.

Although he was teaching soldiers in the UK, his mind unexpectedly transported him back to Afghanistan. Only the murmurs of his concerned students brought him back to the present.

Episodes like this illustrate how someone can unconsciously re-experience traumatic events despite standing in front of a classroom. This is what I call cognitive immobility. Cognitive immobility can affect anyone who has lived through a traumatic, or even affectionate, experience associated with a particular place, relationship, or life experience.

Cognitive immobility can result in someone having a sense of stressful psychological entrapment in which they consciously or unconsciously returns to the past, mentally recreating experiences tied to places they once lived in or visited.

For AJ and many veterans in the United States and the United Kingdom, returning home was supposed to mark the beginning of a more peaceful life—except it often felt like they had never left the battlefield. They experienced what I describe as mental immobilisation in the past, one of the defining features of cognitive immobility. However, not everyone who has been to war will experience cognitive immobility, even though many ex-soldiers may develop post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

article continues after advertisement

According to Charan Ranganath, emotionally charged experiences can leave lasting marks on our memory because they carry information that may help us recognise danger, adapt to similar situations, and survive and flourish. Such experiences may come from bereavement, divorce, retirement, imprisonment, military service, or a painful disappointment or event when some have to leave a homeland, family, loved ones, or a cherished relationship because of circumstances beyond their control.

When the War Comes Home

A 2013 BBC documentary reported that, in 2012, more than 50 UK soldiers died by suicide. This figure is higher than the number of British soldiers killed by the Taliban in Afghanistan that year. The picture is similarly troubling in the United States. According to the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs’ 2025 report, 6,398 veterans died by suicide in 2023.

For many ex-soldiers, leaving the battlefield does not mean leaving the war behind. Some continue to relive combat long after returning home—which can result in severe loneliness alongside persistent emotional pain and mental health issues, while also feeling that those around them cannot fully understand the psychological burden they carry.

The UK military has introduced a range of evidence-based treatments for trauma, including trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), and eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR). According to the Guardian report, AJ underwent EMDR as part of his treatment.

Yet one of the challenges is that these approaches do not always provide answers for everyone. Some ex-soldiers continue to struggle despite receiving appropriate treatment, suggesting that PTSD may not fully explain their experiences. This is where cognitive immobility may offer an additional perspective. As I have argued elsewhere, "PTSD may be one pathway into cognitive immobility."

If we want to better understand how experiences in war zones can continue to affect veterans after they return home, we may need to look beyond PTSD alone and consider whether some of them remain cognitively anchored to the places and experiences they left behind. Doing so may help us better understand "how the past continues to organise a person’s present, shaping how they think, feel, behave, and understand who they are."

article continues after advertisement

An ex-soldier may experience nightmares, and other symptoms associated with PTSD while able to build a meaningful life after returning from the war zone. Another may experience similar symptoms but also remain mentally and emotionally anchored to the war zone itself. In that case, the defining feature is not only the traumatic memories but an enduring cognitive attachment to the past.

Recognising this difference may help us distinguish between those who are haunted by memories of war but live in the present cognitively and those whose minds have never really left the battlefield, even after they receive effective treatment for PTSD.

Healing Means Accepting the Past and Living in the Present

Just like AJ, who struggled with re-experiencing past events in the present, many of us also go through life without realising that our past experiences continue to shape our thoughts, feelings, behaviours, and relationships today.

AJ eventually found ways to begin healing. So can anyone who feels unable to let go of painful experiences from the past. Healing begins when we recognise that although the past cannot be changed, it does not have to dictate how we continue to live.

item.title: Will Old Professors Be Forgotten in the Artificial Intelligence Era?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Will Old Professors Be Forgotten in the Artificial Intelligence Era?

Personal Perspective: An interdisciplinary approach will help academics in the age of AI.

Posted August 17, 2026

Key points
  • Specialization advanced science, but also fragmented our understanding of complex scientific problems.
  • AI may become part of extended cognitive system, changing how we learn.
  • Future scientists need breadth alongside depth to recognize meaningful cross-disciplinary connections.

When I was a student, our professors often told us that human life is not long enough to master the enormous amount of knowledge produced by science. Their advice was simple: choose one subject, go deep into it, and try to understand it as well as possible. This advice was completely reasonable. As scientific knowledge expanded, it became impossible for one person to know everything. Biology became divided into molecular biology, genetics, biochemistry, physiology, neuroscience, immunology, microbiology, and many other fields. The same happened in almost every area of science.

Specialization Both Advanced and Fragmented Science

Specialization gave us enormous scientific progress. But it also created another problem: We became very good at understanding pieces of reality while becoming less capable of seeing the whole.

It is like "The Elephant in the Dark." Several people examine an elephant in darkness. Each person touches a different part of the elephant and describes it. The problem is not that any of them is wrong; rather, each person may believe that the part they have experienced represents the whole animal. Something similar may have happened to modern science.

A scientist may spend twenty years studying one molecular pathway, one receptor, one microorganism, one brain region, or a particular gene. The knowledge can be deep and completely correct. However, many important problems in biology and medicine are not limited to a single pathway, organ, or discipline.

Aging, cancer, obesity, diabetes, consciousness, and human behavior are examples of complex systems in which multiple levels of biological processes and environmental factors interact. Perhaps the problem is not that we do not know enough. Perhaps sometimes we know too much about separate parts and too little about how the parts are connected [1].

Artificial intelligence may change the situation

For centuries, this specialization was partly forced on us because the human brain could not contain all human knowledge. But something has changed. AI can now access enormous amounts of information from different disciplines almost simultaneously. It can summarize scientific papers, explain mathematical models, write computer code, perform statistical analyses, translate technical information, and help us explore subjects far outside our original training. This changes the value of memorizing knowledge. We no longer need to keep all these details and complex calculations in our own minds.

The Extended Mind theory

More than two decades ago, Andy Clark and David Chalmers proposed the idea of the "extended mind." Their famous thought experiment involved a person with Alzheimer's disease who uses a notebook to remember information needed to navigate the world. If the notebook reliably stores information and the person uses it as an integral part of their cognitive process, why should we insist that it is completely outside the cognitive system? This concept now raises a question: Can AI capacities now be considered a part of our mind?

article continues after advertisement

If I can ask an AI system to retrieve a complex equation, find relevant literature, analyze my statistical data, or compare theories from different disciplines, then part of my cognitive activity no longer takes place only inside my brain. Instead of trying to store every piece of information, I can invest more of my cognitive capacity in understanding concepts, mechanisms, patterns, relationships, and questions [2].

An uncomfortable question for academia

Academic institutions have understandably been cautious about the use of AI. They are concerned about plagiarism, fabricated references, incorrect information, and the possibility that students or researchers may submit work they do not fully understand. These concerns are legitimate. However, I believe we sometimes mix two different things: There is a significant difference between asking AI to do our thinking for us and using AI to assist with tasks that free our minds to think more comprehensively.

If we use AI to find a formula that we understand, help us to write R code, translate a technical paragraph, identify relevant papers, or test whether an argument has a weakness, and then critically evaluate the results, have we really abandoned intellectual responsibility? We do not normally consider it academic misconduct when a scientist uses a calculator, statistical software, a search engine, or a reference manager. The important question should not simply be whether AI was used. The important question is: What part of the intellectual responsibility remains with the human researcher? It is plausible that academia will eventually have to confront this question more seriously.

From specialists to systemic thinkers

I do not believe specialists will totally disappear. We will still need them. If AI proposes a connection between two biological phenomena, someone with deep knowledge must be able to determine whether that connection is meaningful or simply a coincidence. But perhaps the future will favor people who combine depth with breadth.

article continues after advertisement

Imagine a scientist who understands the basic principles of several fields: metabolism, neuroscience, microbiology, immunology, evolution, and statistics. This person may not remember every formula or technical detail from each field. But when a problem appears, AI can help retrieve the necessary details. More importantly, this person may recognize something that a highly specialized scientist does not immediately see because each discipline has developed its own language and literature. Perhaps these apparently different phenomena are parts of the same system.

It is not merely about knowing many things; it is about recognizing relationships between concepts that are typically studied separately. This does not mean that AI cannot make such connections. In fact, AI can generate numerous connections, likely more than any individual human can.

However, generating a connection is not the same as understanding its meaning. AI can indicate that two phenomena are correlated, identify similarities between theories, and suggest unexpected hypotheses. The human role may increasingly become deciding which of these connections are meaningful, which are coincidental, and which warrant further scientific investigation. Perhaps the challenge will move from finding connections to understanding which connections matter.

Now, the question is: what will we do with this new freedom? Will we use AI to produce answers faster? Or will we use it to see connections that specialization prevented us from seeing?

Perhaps the next scientific revolution will be a return to the discipline that originally gave rise to all sciences: philosophy. Philosophy addresses holistic questions about the world and fundamental human concerns. Most PhD students, and even professors, have forgotten that "PhD" stands for Doctor of Philosophy. Being grounded in this discipline may help academicians to see connections between phenomena and answer the unresolved questions within their fields. A philosophical perspective encourages scientists to seek meaningful connections, evaluate their significance, and explore what constitutes a meaningful relationship between ideas.

item.title: Awareness of AI Doesn't Fail. It's Never Been Tested
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Awareness of AI Doesn't Fail. It's Never Been Tested

Researchers claim AI awareness doesn't protect us. But it hasn't been studied.

Posted August 17, 2026

Key points
  • Warning people that AI flatters them reduces trust but not its power to change their minds.
  • Researchers call this "sycophancy blindness": noticing flattery doesn't stop it from working.
  • One-time warnings are not the same as ongoing, real-time self-awareness.
  • Clinicians risk abandoning a real tool if they mistake this research approach as proof awareness fails.

We keep telling people to be "aware" of what AI does. New research suggests it barely helps.

In "Individual-Level Interventions Against Sycophantic AI Reduce Its Appeal But Not Its Persuasiveness," Ye et al. (2026) warned users that an AI was sycophantic: flattering and overly agreeable. It was the kind of AI that tells you what you want to hear.

The warnings worked, sort of. People trusted the AI less. Enjoyed it less. Rated it as less objective. These are good signs. If using AI feels easy and effortless, it's probably impacting you more than you realize. And not in a good way.

But regardless of the warning, AI changed their minds anyway. Just as much as if they had never been warned at all.

The researchers call it "sycophancy blindness." Even people who noticed the AI was validating everyone were still moved when it validated them. We see the same thing when people are told outright they're talking to an AI and not a real person (Joshi et al., 2026). It affects them anyway.

Three Risk Areas of Using AI

Cheng and Jurafsky (2026) found that AI affirms user behavior at a substantially higher rate than humans do in comparable conversations. They also reported that people who received those sycophantic AI responses became less willing to apologize or repair after interpersonal conflict. That's a marriage, a friendship, a working relationship, absorbing the cost of an AI that agreed with someone when a human would have pushed back.

Self-awareness is the key to healthy AI use
Source: Merlin Lightpainting

The impacts aren’t isolated to conflict repair. The risks of interacting with AI show up across three areas. Emotionally, validation from AI shapes decisions and confidence in ways people don't fully register in the moment. Socially, a 12-month study found using chatbots for companionship predicted increased loneliness four months later, and feeling lonelier predicted more chatbot use four months after that (Folk & Dunn, 2026). Cognitively, just ten minutes of AI assistance was enough to make people give up faster on their own problem-solving afterward, a quick erosion of independent effort (Liu et al., 2025).

This is what's actually at stake when AI shapes how we think, feel, and connect. A single warning, delivered once before anyone starts using it, was never going to hold up against effects like these. That's why I disagree when researchers call this a failure of awareness.

What actually failed was one-time education, a fact delivered once, not the ongoing, active noticing that real awareness requires. And if clinicians read this study as proof that awareness doesn't work, we lose a real way of helping our clients.

The whole reason I developed the AI Awareness Arc is that I think real self-awareness and intensive education are what let us stand our ground with AI, to use it safely and effectively.

What Self-Awareness Really Is

When I say self-awareness, I mean noticing our own thoughts, feelings, and experiences in real time, or as close to it as we can get.

It's noticing what AI does and how it makes us feel, so we can respond in the moment instead of being swayed by the interaction without realizing it. It's being able to point at the screen and say, "That's it agreeing with me again," or "There's that closing hook to keep me engaged."

Self-awareness is seeing the question AI so often asks, checking in with ourselves, and deciding whether we want to answer that question, address something else, or decide we got what we needed and we're finished. It's noticing how AI is shifting our thinking, our certainty, our willingness to sit with disagreement or discomfort.

This study shows, as others have, that simple education, like a warning label or a one-off message, won't be enough to offset the impact of AI. A warning sign on a car wouldn't be enough to get us to drive safely either.

We need driver's ed-style training: Real instruction on what AI is, and live practice with it, so people learn the risks it carries and how to navigate it safely.

item.title: Why Patients Decline Effective Therapy
item.description:
Hypnosis

Why Patients Decline Effective Therapy

Reframing hypnosis and rethinking informed consent.

Posted August 17, 2026

Key points
  • Misconceptions about hypnosis are often based on inaccurate portrayals in popular media.
  • Some patients remain wary of hypnosis even after misconceptions are corrected.
  • It is worthwhile to think about the ethics of using hypnotic techniques while avoiding the term “hypnosis."

When clinicians introduce hypnosis as a possible therapy, they sometimes encounter misconceptions held by their clients about the nature of hypnosis. These are often based on inaccurate portrayals in popular media of how hypnosis might be misused.

Frequent misconceptions include the ideas that hypnosis involves the clinician’s taking control of a patient’s mind, that it induces sleep, and that it is an abnormal or unusual state.

Source: Nikki Zalewski/Shutterstock

For some patients, the term “hypnosis” feels exciting and they are eager to learn how to utilize it.

However, even after clinicians address misconceptions, and explain that hypnosis involves the use of imagination that is controlled by the patients themselves, some patients and/or their family members remain wary. Reasons for this hesitancy may include:

  • Religious or cultural beliefs
  • A past negative experience with hypnosis such as might have occurred during a stage show
  • A fear that something might be revealed of which they are consciously aware, but that they would rather keep private;
  • A fear of bringing inner conflicts into conscious awareness, as may occur in patients dealing with traumatic events
  • Mistrust of health care providers
  • Worry that responsiveness to hypnosis proves that the patient is weak-willed
  • Disbelief in the potential efficacy of hypnosis
  • Lack of self-confidence that they would be able to use hypnosis properly
  • Disinterest in investing effort into learning a new thinking pattern
  • A wish to retain a symptom as it serves a beneficial purpose (previously thought of as secondary gain). For example, at a subconscious level a teenager may want to remain short of breath that precludes vigorous physical activity so that they are not forced by their family to participate in an athletic endeavor they dislike.

Some patients and their families can be prompted to verbalize the reasons they remain hesitant about hypnosis, in which case the clinician can better address their concerns.

For example, reassurance that clinical hypnosis is different from stage hypnosis can alleviate some of the fears that might have arisen because of a previous negative experience.

Some patients continue to decline the opportunity to learn about hypnosis even after additional reassurance. In other situations, clinicians may be aware that their patients will not be receptive to therapy with hypnosis prior to introducing this tool because of the culture or religion to which their patients belong.

Generally, in such instances, a non-hypnotic approach to the presenting symptom should be undertaken.

However, there are some conditions for which hypnosis has been shown to be an excellent first-line therapy including habit cough, headaches, insomnia, irritable bowel syndrome, and vocal cord dysfunction.

This presents a clinical dilemma regarding how to best approach treatment of these conditions for which hypnosis has been demonstrated to have clear efficacy.

Perhaps, therapeutic suggestions can be given without calling them “hypnotic.” For instance, consider the following terms that may be more palatable:

  • Visualize how it would feel to be healthier.
  • Use guided imagery to show the mind how to heal.
  • Use your imagination to help yourself.
  • Practice picturing yourself in your mind without the problem that used to be there.
  • Teach your mind how to better control itself and your body.
  • Learn how to ask your inner self to help you.

A Question of Informed Consent

It is worthwhile to think about the ethics of avoiding the term “hypnosis.”

If a clinician uses hypnotic techniques but does not label them as such, it could be argued that the patient has not been given sufficient information to provide informed consent for the therapy.

On the other hand, if a patient’s difficulty with the term “hypnosis” prevents them from accepting effective treatment, I believe it is a clinician’s responsibility to figure out how to provide such treatment.

As long as the patient is clearly informed of the steps in this therapy, I believe that the duty to provide informed consent has been fulfilled.

For instance, a patient could be told that they would be taught to achieve a calm state by imagining a relaxing place of their choice (visualization). They would then be taught to trigger that relaxed state by recalling their relaxing place.

Thus, informed consent can rest on an accurate understanding of the therapeutic experience rather than on the acceptance or rejection of a single word.

If a patient later states that they discovered they were not informed that the techniques they were taught were hypnotic in nature, a clinician might point out that there is no universally accepted definition of hypnosis.

Further, while hypnosis can involve focused attention, imagination, expectation, and therapeutic suggestion, these processes are common for other practices including meditation, guided imagery, psychotherapy, athletic visualization, and sometimes even prayer.

Point to Ponder

When MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) scans were first introduced, they were called NMR (nuclear magnetic resonance) scans. Unfortunately, the word “nuclear” prevented many patients from accepting this new therapy.

When the name change took place, and patients were informed that no radiation was involved, MRIs became widely acceptable and have become an invaluable tool in medicine (Goldberg, 2007).

Sometimes, a name change is key for a therapy to be adopted.

item.title: Exploring the Nuances of Well-Being
item.description:
Education

Exploring the Nuances of Well-Being

Advancing knowledge across countries and facets.

Posted August 17, 2026

Key points
  • Knowledge of flourishing expands by systematically studying various aspects across countries.
  • Patterns of flourishing often differ depending on the aspect of well-being examined.
  • Patterns of flourishing also often differ across countries.
  • We need a better understanding of what is universal and what is context-specific.

The Global Flourishing Study has allowed us to gain insight into the distribution and determinants of flourishing from over 200,000 participants in 22 countries around the world. We’ve begun to learn what patterns are more universal versus more context-specific. By using a common set of methodologies across studies, we can have more confidence that different relations for different aspects of well-being (e.g. happiness vs. meaning vs. relationships) are not methodological artifacts, but are giving real insight.

This work has been facilitated not only by the strengths of the study and a common set of methodologies but by partnerships with journals to facilitate coordinated publication of the work. Our Global Flourishing Study special collection with the Springer-Nature journals has hosted a series of papers on demographic relations with different well-being outcomes across countries, and another on childhood predictors of different aspects of well-being. Our partnership with the International Journal of Wellbeing has provided a series of country-specific commentaries on these results. We are grateful for these partnerships and believe they have allowed for the more rapid advancement of knowledge, an advance that likewise was only made possible through the devoted work over many years of a highly collaborative interdisciplinary research team.

Recent Critiques of the Global Flourishing Study

This approach, and our work, have recently come under some critique by an economist, David Blanchflower. Some of the critiques are quite reasonable, for example, concerning methodological issues, such as so-called “mode effects” wherein individuals may be inclined to answer differently depending on whether they are contacted via telephone versus online. We have noted this as a limitation in our work, and are continuing to explore these issues. Awareness of such study limitations helps us appropriately weight evidence.

However, other critiques are broader, for example, that “It is well documented in hundreds of papers that well-being and ill-being are correlated with age, income, education, labor force and immigrant status, religion and political beliefs… There is nothing much new under the sun.” And also, especially in reference to our series of country-specific papers, that: “All results have previously been published by the same authors.” These critiques, we believe, are less reasonable, and in a response paper recently published in the International Journal of Wellbeing, we lay out why. We transparently provide the entire vision for, and research infrastructure of, our core Global Flourishing Study research team. We describe our approach to advancing knowledge through coordinated research reports with a common methodology, grounded in principles of multi-purpose epidemiologic cohort designs, outcome-wide templates examining numerous outcomes simultaneously, and multidimensional conceptualizations of flourishing, and how years of planning went into developing this coordinated approach to the design and analysis of the Global Flourishing Study.

Responding: Learning What Is Universal and What Is Context-Specific

Undoubtedly, there has been tremendous learning on the topic of well-being in prior decades, from numerous investigators, across numerous disciplines, and these have indeed demonstrated that “well-being and ill-being are correlated with age, income, education, labor force and immigrant status, religion and political beliefs.” However, much of this literature has been (i) carried out in Western contexts, (ii) has concerned narrow measures of well-being such as happiness, or life satisfaction/evaluation, and (iii) has made use of cross-sectional data, rendering causal inferences more challenging. What the Global Flourishing Study is allowing us to do is to examine how patterns vary across countries, including in non-Western contexts; to examine numerous aspects of well-being, not just happiness/life satisfaction; and, over time, as the waves of data accumulate, to try to use the longitudinal panel data to draw causal inferences.

There is only “nothing much new under the sun” if one were to think that all the patterns for different aspects of well-being are the same, and are the same across all countries. But this simply is not the case. As we note in our response, in most countries, flourishing is increasing with education, but it’s the opposite in Australia and Hong Kong. In many countries, flourishing is now increasing with age, but in Poland and Tanzania, it is decreasing. In many countries, married individuals report higher flourishing than those who are single, but in India and Tanzania it is the reverse. These patterns should not be seen as outliers to some supposedly universal law across countries. They are important results in their own right, relevant to millions of people, or, in the case of India, over a billion people. The International Journal of Wellbeing country-specific commentaries were intended to provide reflection on such country-specific results, rather than only those aggregated across all countries.

Patterns also differ with different aspects of well-being. For example, at the country level, life evaluation is increasing with GDP/capita; however, strikingly, with meaning in life, the pattern is the reverse. Many countries in the study now have patterns with life satisfaction that are increasing-with-age or slightly “J-shaped,” but in many of the same countries, the same patterns do not hold with self-rated physical health (though strikingly in America they do). As another example, unsurprisingly, childhood abuse or neglect predicts worse adult well-being across a host of outcomes, but not all. These same adverse childhood experiences predict higher levels of volunteering, charitable giving, and informal helping, and strikingly, more frequent adult experiences of beauty. All of this is missed if one does not separately examine different aspects of well-being across countries. We ultimately need a better understanding of which patterns seem to be universal, and which are context-specific, and how this varies across countries, and why. That is precisely what our series of research papers is beginning to attempt to do.

Growing in Wisdom

Nevertheless, in light of the totality of all these studies, Blanchflower offers the perhaps reasonable critique, “We are never told which of the 68 variables we should focus on and why.” The questions of “What is most important?”, and “What do we ultimately learn?”, and “What are we to do?” are essential. We ultimately want to grow not only in knowledge, but in wisdom. In our flagship paper, in reflecting on the big-picture takeaways, we pointed towards how different countries are flourishing in different ways, the declining well-being of youth, the role of religion, and the complexities of adversity. Undoubtedly other authors would have drawn attention to other points, and it is in part for this reason that the entire Global Flourishing Study dataset has been made open access, so that others can provide their own insights from it. We have also engaged with groups of policy-makers, academics, and interested individuals from many of the participating countries to better understand their perspectives, to gain insight, and to give the quantitative results greater texture. The International Journal of Wellbeing series of country-specific commentaries was intended to give authors from each of the participating countries a voice as well. Further learning will inevitably come from integrating the results of the Global Flourishing Study with other research through meta-analyses and systematic reviews. While the path to wisdom is not always clear, we hope that these various efforts, and others, and further critiques, will, over time, help us to discern what is most important, and better ways to promote flourishing across countries. This is not the work of one research group, but ultimately of all people.

item.title: Can Our Brain Grasp What’s Happening to the Earth?
item.description:
Environment

Can Our Brain Grasp What’s Happening to the Earth?

A Personal Perspective: Why have people habituated to the warnings about climate change?

Posted August 17, 2026

Key points
  • Scientists have been sounding alarms about human impact on climate since the early 1800s.
  • The brain evolved to focus on the present, food, avoiding death and procreating; climate change is slow.
  • Apathy is a defensive mechanism by our neolithic brain.

I’ve been reading published climate science literature for the past 20 years. The warnings about what is currently happening to our planet, and the predictions about what is going to happen, are now clearly defined and well supported by evidence. Scientists are sounding the alarms, but no one seems to notice.

The alarms have been blaring for a very long time. In 1824, Joseph Fourier proposed that the atmosphere traps heat; in 1856, Eunice Newton Foote demonstrated CO₂’s warming effect on the planet. In 1896, Svante Arrhenius, a Swedish chemist and physicist, calculated the greenhouse effect and estimated that doubling CO₂ could raise global temperatures. In 1898, he explicitly linked rising CO₂ from industrial processes to a future “greenhouse effect” that could make the Earth’s climate “unendurable,” and was the first to warn that human activity could cause long-term climate change. Climate change occurs very slowly; 200 years later, we are witnessing the accuracy of their predictions.

Is anyone concerned?

The people who express the most concern are the people who will be most impacted. Younger adults report higher climate anxiety, with 49% of Gen Z and 39% of Millennials feeling anxious about their future. Older adults, particularly those aged 70 and above, who will not live long enough to witness the consequences of climate change, are much less worried, with only 22% expressing high concern.

Climate scientists face a difficult irony: they are predicting disastrous consequences for our planet, yet most people’s eyes glaze over when they are made aware. Climate disasters, such as apocalyptic fires across the world, widespread flooding and endless droughts, are now the lead news stories every evening. Heat-related deaths have more than doubled since 2019, reflecting the increasing frequency and intensity of heat waves due to climate change. Our world is becoming less hospitable, and we seem apathetic to it. I’ve given up trying to engage people in conversation about the topic.

Why are we so apathetic?

For most people, at least for now, climate change is a problem with the outside world. We can see the smoke from fires in Canada and witness the flooding in the Midwest and droughts in the Southwest (Lake Powell, a vital reservoir on the Utah-Arizona border, has now fallen to its lowest level ever), but then we turn away to deal with more pressing personal issues. Also, the changes that many of us have witnessed have been unfolding very slowly. Our brain evolved to focus on the present and our need to find food, avoid injury or death and procreate. Climate change is not a “today problem.” There have always been climate-related catastrophes that are mostly just experienced by a few and then ignored by the majority. It’s not easy for our brain to notice the significant but gradual changes in the intensity, the frequency, or the widespread impact of these changes over time. Charts prepared by scientists that accurately document what is happening are mostly ignored. Why?

Author Robert A. Heinlein wrote that “Man is not a rational animal; he is a rationalizing animal.” He argued that we humans do not think carefully or logically, rather we are driven by our emotions and fears to justify beliefs that logic does not support. Our response to climate change is a case in point. Our collective response to COVID is another case in point. No one wanted to wear masks or change their daily habits to avoid an invisible danger. As soon as we felt safe, our apathy to the danger disappeared, and these measures were abandoned in order to feel a sense of normalcy again. There were global consequences to our apathy. Between January 2020 and December 2021, about 14.9 million excess deaths occurred globally. This figure includes both direct COVID-19 deaths and indirect deaths from other causes that occurred when healthcare systems were overwhelmed by people who, unnecessarily, contracted the COVID virus.

Moreover, there are predispositions among certain types of people that make them particularly unwilling to wrestle with global warming in ways that paralleled their response to the pandemic. People with an aversion to government regulations (such as being forced to wear masks, close their businesses or avoid crowds) apply the same logic to global climate change. Studies have shown that political conservatives are less likely to accept the science of climate change or policies proposed to mitigate this unfurling catastrophe. Conservatives are more likely to see the world as fixed and unmalleable, in the sense that what they (as human beings) do to it will have little impact on diminishing the impacts of climate change (Chan & Faria, 2022). They blame the current climate on disproven astronomical phenomenon.

Psychologists have pointed to a number of brain "flaws" to help explain this climate apathy, with concepts like loss aversion, optimism bias, and our desire for instant gratification being proposed. To me, these explanations are gross oversimplifications that ignore facts about how our brain evolved and how it learned to survive. In my opinion, the best explanation is that the human brain has a hard time recognizing and understanding incremental change. Our only solution is to rely on scientists and their charts to help us see what’s hidden in front of us.

As more people are impacted by the destructive manifestations of our warming planet, more people are forced to care. Unfortunately, we’ve wasted a lot of time since those early warnings. The first documented public warnings from scientists to oil executives came in 1959, with private industry knowledge emerging in the 1960s. By the 1970s, internal research had confirmed the link between fossil fuel use and climate change. The oil industry internally acknowledged (their documents were leaked to the press) that its product would cause catastrophic changes to our environment; their solution was to weaponize doubt in the 1980s to ensure their profits. The same approach worked well for the tobacco companies in the 1970s. Some people still believe the propaganda of oil companies.

What can be done? One action we can take is to keep climate change top of our mind when heading to the voting booth. In addition, we need to accept that our apathy does not imply that we don’t care. Apathy is one of our brain’s defensive mechanisms. We all need to allow ourselves grace in how we deal with a problem of unprecedented proportion using a brain that first started to evolve in the lower Paleolithic period.

item.title: Autism Is Not a Crutch
item.description:
Autism

Autism Is Not a Crutch

The danger of mistaking autistic strengths for an absence of disability.

Posted August 17, 2026

Key points
  • Giftedness can mask autism, but it does not erase disability.
  • The stereotypical image of autism represents only one presentation of a highly diverse spectrum.
  • Autistic people should not have to fail before receiving support.
  • Rising autism diagnoses do not automatically prove overdiagnosis.

There seems to be much debate over the diagnosis and assessment of autism. Historically, autism diagnoses were often reserved for very young children who had severe communication difficulties that frequently overlapped with intellectual disability. This became the stereotypical presentation of autism. With the publication of the fifth edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5), several diagnoses that had previously existed within the pervasive developmental disorders category were combined under the diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). This change, together with increased self-advocacy among autistic adults, greater professional awareness, and growing access to information about autism beyond traditional stereotypes, contributed to a substantial increase in autism diagnoses.

Yet a broad segment of clinical and popular culture believes this increase in diagnoses is due to overdiagnosis. Those of us who are late-diagnosed autistic people deal with this perspective regularly. People frequently tell us that we “don’t seem autistic.” If you are autistic and well-spoken, intelligent, or gifted in a particular area, this group of people will argue that you are not representative of the “real” autistic population. In The Independent, Dame Uta Frith recently argued that “today, anyone of any age or intelligence level can be diagnosed with autism if they meet certain criteria” (Frith, as cited in Newton, 2026). Although this statement is literally consistent with current diagnostic criteria, the article’s headline—“anyone can have autism now”—invites a much broader and more dismissive interpretation.

Research reviewed by Uddin (2022) offers several possible explanations for differences in how autism presents. Some research suggests that autistic cognitive traits—such as heightened perception, detail-focused processing, and strong systemizing—may contribute to gifted or savant-like abilities, creating a twice-exceptional profile of significant strengths alongside genuine disabilities. These strengths may mask support needs, while challenges with processing speed, executive functioning, sensory regulation, or communication may hide the person’s giftedness.

This framework does not divide autism into separate “types,” but describes several cognitive patterns that may produce different combinations of strengths and disabilities. Enhanced perceptual functioning may contribute to exceptional visual, auditory, musical, spatial, or pattern-recognition abilities; hyper-systemizing may support advanced skills in mathematics, technology, language, calendars, classification, or any subject governed by rules; and detail-focused processing may help someone detect small differences and achieve extraordinary accuracy, even when integrating information into a broader context is difficult. These patterns may contribute to savant abilities, meaning an exceptionally developed skill in one narrow area; intellectual giftedness, meaning unusually high general reasoning ability; or twice-exceptionality, in which autism and giftedness coexist alongside sensory, communication, executive-function, adaptive, or emotional difficulties.

Because autistic cognition is often uneven or “spiky,” a person may be profoundly talented in one domain while needing substantial support in another. Giftedness can therefore conceal disability, and visible disability can prevent others from recognizing giftedness. Importantly, this framework does not claim that every autistic person is gifted or that autistic people with high support needs possess hidden genius. It proposes that certain autistic processing styles may contribute to exceptional abilities in some individuals and that strengths and disabilities must be assessed separately.

article continues after advertisement

Much research provides support for many of the cognitive patterns reviewed by Uddin. The stereotypical autistic child represents only one possible presentation: a child whose disability and communication differences are highly visible. That child may or may not possess exceptional abilities, just as a speaking or intellectually gifted autistic adult may still have substantial disabilities and support needs.

Every day I see articles, stories, and posts about autism being overdiagnosed and about people using neurodivergence or autism as a crutch or an excuse to escape personal responsibility in some way. Yet this assumption is often based on the belief that people who have exceptional abilities, whether cognitive gifts or savant-like skills, cannot possibly be autistic because of those abilities alone. It does not acknowledge that twice-exceptional autistic people are still autistic. These people still experience autistic sensory, social, communication, and daily struggles, although those experiences and support needs vary from person to person. Along with those struggles, they also carry the burden of expectation. They are expected to live up to their gifts. They are expected to thrive and live the exceptional lives that the ordinary world wants from their savant-like skills. This pressure can be crushing when they are still haunted by sensory, social, communication, and other forms of overload.

I know many twice-exceptional autistic adults. I have known engineers, musicians, artists, and writers who are twice-exceptional. They are remarkable. The outside world does not think they seem autistic, but they still struggle. One artist I know was so exceptional that she skipped a grade. She was always ahead of everyone academically, and her intelligence and exceptional gifts were all anyone could see. Her giftedness obfuscated all the issues she struggled with every day. When she finally melted down and collapsed under the pressure of all the labels, she could never paint again. Her gifts were lost in the avalanche of neurotypical expectations.

article continues after advertisement

Uddin says that twice-exceptional autistic people may possess specialized skills that allow them to make important contributions in education and the workforce while simultaneously experiencing substantial difficulties with social functioning, daily living, and the transition to independence. Their intelligence can cause others to underestimate their disabilities, leaving them without appropriate services, while public misconceptions can contribute to isolation, underemployment, mental-health difficulties, and unmet support needs.

As a twice-exceptional adult, I am always walking a tightrope. I know that people do not see me as struggling. They just see the gifts. They also do not see all the ways I am not exceptional — the ways I am well below the norm, and the ways I struggle daily to live up to even basic expectations. It is easy to see that I can write and create new things, but it is hard to see the many things I hide: my inability to keep up with basic tasks, the way I forget daily responsibilities, and the way I become overwhelmed under pressure. They do not see me meltdown in the grocery store or my inability to read a room or understand things that are not concrete.

Claims that autism is overdiagnosed, used to excuse bad behavior, or something that “anyone can be these days” are dangerous because, as Uddin’s discussion of twice-exceptionality demonstrates, autistic strengths can conceal significant disabilities and support needs; recognizing why someone struggles is not the same as removing personal responsibility.
